summary:
LIMEN — Mission Health Intelligence is a research-oriented software prototype exploring how human performance and behavioural observations can be understood across changing gravity environments.

The project brings together a browser-based sensorimotor adaptation assessment, subjective crew check-ins, longitudinal performance analysis, mission-context records, and a scientific evidence explorer. Its assessment simulates altered visual feedback to observe how a participant adapts to and recovers from a visuomotor perturbation. LIMEN also integrates 1,596 measurement records from three selected datasets across NASA's SpaceX Inspiration4 studies, allowing users to explore retrospective biomedical measurements alongside their original provenance.

A separate synthetic mission environment demonstrates how these capabilities could support mission-level review without mixing fictional data with real observations.

LIMEN aims to make complex human-performance evidence more accessible, traceable, and interpretable, while highlighting the importance of careful measurement and scientific limitations in human spaceflight research.
details:
LIMEN — Mission Health Intelligence

1. Project Overview

LIMEN is a research-oriented software prototype designed to explore human performance, sensorimotor adaptation, and behavioural observations in the context of human spaceflight.

Space missions expose astronauts to changing gravity environments, which can affect how they perceive movement, coordinate actions, and adapt to unfamiliar conditions. Understanding these changes requires more than isolated measurements: it requires the ability to collect observations, preserve their context, examine changes over time, and distinguish measured evidence from interpretation.

LIMEN brings these elements together in an interactive mission-health intelligence environment. It combines browser-based behavioural assessment, subjective crew observations, longitudinal analysis, retrospective NASA biomedical datasets, and an isolated synthetic mission simulation.

2. What Does LIMEN Do?

The platform is organised around three primary operational areas — CONTEXT, OPERATE, and ANALYSE — alongside a separate SIMULATION environment.

CONTEXT — Mission Framing

This area allows users to define mission contexts, record mission events, and explicitly document transitions between mission phases. These records provide context for interpreting observations rather than relying on automatically inferred mission events.

OPERATE — Human Performance Observations

This area contains two major capabilities:

  • Sensorimotor Adaptation Assessment: A browser-based visuomotor task that records participant interaction across four phases: baseline, adaptation, late adaptation, and washout. During adaptation, the visual feedback cursor is rotated 45 degrees clockwise, creating a controlled visual perturbation. The system records pointer trajectories, timing, trial conditions, and derives descriptive behavioural metrics from the collected trials.
  • Crew Check-in: A subjective self-report interface for recording participant observations. These reports are maintained separately from instrument-derived behavioural measurements.

ANALYSE — Evidence and Longitudinal Review

This area provides several complementary tools:

  • Recovery & Reference: Reviews assessment observations and supports comparisons against a personal reference session within the same browser profile.
  • Personal Trends: Displays chronological trends in behavioural measurements and subjective check-ins.
  • Signal Concordance: Allows users to explicitly associate completed assessments with self-reported observations for descriptive comparison.
  • Observations & Events: Organises recorded mission events, transitions, and follow-up review workflows.
  • Scientific Evidence Registry: Provides an organised view of the evidence and its provenance.
  • NASA OSDR Explorer: Enables exploration of selected retrospective biomedical datasets from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.
  • Scientific Methodology and Privacy: Explain the analytical approach, limitations, and browser-local data handling.

SIMULATION — Synthetic Mission Environment

LIMEN also includes a separate fictional mission environment with synthetic astronaut profiles and deterministic mission records. It demonstrates how mission contexts, events, assessments, check-ins, trends, and evidence could be reviewed together in a mission-oriented workflow.

Synthetic records are explicitly labelled and isolated from real operational observations. They are not presented as actual astronaut data.

3. NASA Open Science Data Repository Integration

An important research component of LIMEN is its integration of selected datasets from NASA's SpaceX Inspiration4 studies.

The current explorer includes three measurement collections:

  • Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP): 532 measurement records.
  • Cardiovascular 9-plex: 504 measurement records.
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC): 560 measurement records.

Together, these represent 1,596 measurement records across the three selected collections.

The explorer supports dataset selection, analyte exploration, sample-series visualisation, and source measurement tables. It preserves source identifiers, timepoints, analyte information, units, values, and missing-value information to support transparent exploration.

These are retrospective ground-based preflight and postflight measurements, not continuous in-flight telemetry. LIMEN does not claim that these biomedical records are directly paired with its browser-based behavioural assessments.

4. How Does It Work?

The platform follows a structured evidence workflow:

  1. Define mission context and explicitly record relevant events and transitions.
  2. Collect behavioural observations through the visuomotor assessment.
  3. Record subjective observations separately through crew check-ins.
  4. Derive descriptive metrics from assessment trials.
  5. Review eligible observations through personal trends, reference comparisons, and explicit concordance.
  6. Explore selected NASA biomedical datasets independently through the scientific evidence explorer.
  7. Use the isolated synthetic mission environment to demonstrate how these capabilities could fit into a broader mission-review workflow.

This approach prioritises traceability, separation of evidence types, and transparency over unsupported predictions.

5. Technology Stack and Development Tools

LIMEN was developed using:

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Interactive 3D visualisation: Three.js, React Three Fiber, and WebGL.
  • Data processing: Python and JavaScript/TypeScript.
  • Data representation: Structured JSON, deterministic data-building workflows, and provenance metadata.
  • Visual analytics: Interactive charts, time-series views, and scientific data exploration.
  • Testing and quality assurance: Automated tests, TypeScript checks, ESLint, data-pipeline validation, and production builds.
  • Version control and deployment: GitHub and Vercel.

The platform also uses browser-local persistence for operational observations, while its synthetic simulation environment remains isolated from operational records.

6. Creativity and Innovation

LIMEN's central idea is to connect several kinds of human-performance evidence within one coherent environment rather than presenting isolated charts or disconnected datasets.

Its creative aspects include:

  • A visually immersive, interactive Earth and atmospheric landing experience.
  • A browser-based visuomotor perturbation task that makes sensorimotor adaptation observable.
  • Separate handling of subjective reports and behavioural measurements.
  • Personal reference comparisons and longitudinal review.
  • Exploration of real NASA biomedical measurement records with preserved provenance.
  • A fictional mission simulation that demonstrates an integrated mission-review workflow without misrepresenting synthetic information as real astronaut data.

The platform is designed to make research concepts understandable through interactive exploration while maintaining a clear distinction between observation, analysis, and interpretation.

7. Benefits and Intended Impact

LIMEN provides a prototype framework for exploring how behavioural observations, mission context, subjective reports, and retrospective biomedical evidence can be organised and reviewed together.

Its potential value lies in:

  • Making human-performance research concepts more accessible through interactive visualisation.
  • Demonstrating how sensorimotor adaptation can be studied using a repeatable browser-based task.
  • Supporting longitudinal observation and within-profile comparisons.
  • Making scientific datasets easier to explore while preserving their original context.
  • Encouraging transparent interpretation by clearly distinguishing real observations, retrospective research data, and synthetic simulation records.

In the longer term, the project could be extended with validated experimental protocols, additional spaceflight datasets, and appropriately designed research collaborations.

8. Scientific Considerations and Limitations

LIMEN is an exploratory research prototype, not a clinical or operational astronaut assessment system.

The browser-based task is not a laboratory-grade vestibular measurement protocol and does not directly measure neural activity or diagnose impairment. Its metrics are descriptive and are not clinically validated measures of recovery or astronaut readiness.

Comparisons are restricted to eligible observations within the same browser profile and compatible protocols. NASA OSDR measurements are explored independently and are not used to claim paired biomarker-behaviour relationships. The synthetic mission environment is fictional and is not connected to actual astronaut records.

These distinctions are fundamental to LIMEN's design: the platform aims to support careful exploration of evidence without overstating what that evidence can establish.

9. Final Vision

LIMEN explores a central question in human spaceflight: how can we better understand human performance when the environment in which the human body operates changes?

By bringing together behavioural assessment, mission context, longitudinal observation, scientific datasets, and interactive simulation, LIMEN presents a foundation for more accessible and evidence-aware exploration of human performance between worlds.
